metadata.note: Yes - Chambersburg, Pennsylvania had passenger rail, and a lot of it. Steam trains from November 1837 to 1961 (124 years) and four electric interurban routes radiating from the square between 1905 and 1932. The trunk was the Cumberland Valley Railroad, Harrisburg-Carlisle-Shippensburg-Chambersburg (opened 1837) and on south through Greencastle to Hagerstown (1841/1860), controlled by the Pennsylvania Railroad from 1859 and bought outright on 2 June 1919. Local passenger service ended in 1952; the last passenger train through Chambersburg was the overnight New York-Harrisburg-Hagerstown-Roanoke run the PRR worked with the Norfolk and Western, removed in 1961. The Chambersburg-Waynesboro branch (Mont Alto Rail Road, 1872) lost its passengers on 28 June 1933. RULE 5 NOTE: the Chambersburg-Hagerstown line is deliberately NOT drawn between 1841 and 1860. The Franklin Railroad that built it sold its locomotives around 1841 and was worked by horses through the 1840s and 1850s, so those years are animal haulage and out of scope; the line reappears when it was rebuilt for locomotives in 1860. RULE 1 NOTE: nothing here is drawn past the end of its passenger service. The Waynesboro Branch carried freight to 1972-76 and the Chambersburg main line still does today as Norfolk Southern's Lurgan District, but those years are not drawn. The Western Maryland's Lurgan Branch, which crosses Franklin County a few miles west of Chambersburg through Marion, is not included: it did not serve Chambersburg and its passenger history was not researched here.

not_yet_sourced: Every headway_min in this file is an estimate. No Cumberland Valley or PRR public timetable was consulted; the numbers say roughly how frequent the service felt, not what was scheduled.
The exact end date of the last New York-Roanoke train: 1961 (PHMC marker, pennsyrr.com) vs 10 June 1962 for the N&W's own Hagerstown-Roanoke trains (railfanguides.us).
When horse power actually began on the Franklin Railroad: 1841 (pennsyrr.com) vs 1844 (secondary account).
Whether the Chambersburg and Shippensburg Railway quit in 1926 or 1928 - the Wikipedia article contradicts itself.
Whether Chambersburg had a purely local street railway distinct from the three interurbans; the interurban cars used the town streets, but no separate city system was researched.
Whether the Western Maryland's Lurgan Branch through Marion carried passengers, and if so between which points and in which years.

properties.speed_source: estimated: 1830s-1910s main-line steam on a level valley route; the PHMC marker claims trains regularly exceeded 90 mph on parts of this line in the early 1900s, but no timetable was checked, so this average is unsourced.

segments.note: The Cumberland Valley Railroad opened from White Hill (opposite Harrisburg) to Carlisle in August 1837 and through to Chambersburg in November 1837, giving Chambersburg its first passenger trains. It ran one of the industry's first sleeping cars from 1838, and until the PRR main line was finished in 1854 the fastest Pittsburgh-Philadelphia trip was by stage to Chambersburg and train from there. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap over the surviving Cumberland Valley alignment: NS Shippensburg Secondary (Harrisburg-Carlisle, in service), the Cumberland Valley Rail Trail on the abandoned main (Newville-Shippensburg) and the NS Lurgan District into Chambersburg. 84.8 km / 52.7 mi traced against a documented 52 mi Harrisburg-Chambersburg. 6.2 km of that (7%) is straight-line where the right of way is erased and untagged: 3.30 km near 40.193,-77.293 and 1.48 km near 40.200,-77.251 (both between Carlisle and Newville, where the ROW has been ploughed back into farmland), 0.65 km through Shippensburg and 0.74 km at the Chambersburg end. One train each way per night - the 1440-minute headway is that, not an estimate of a clock-face service. NOTE: this draws the 1837-41 strap-rail Franklin Railroad on the alignment as rebuilt in 1860 and since realigned - the corridor is right, the exact 1837 alignment is not traced.

segments.note: The Franklin Railroad opened south from Chambersburg to Greencastle in 1837 - oak stringers topped with iron bar, worked by the company's own steam locomotives. Those locomotives were sold about 1841 when the Cumberland Valley took over working the road, and the Franklin was then run by HORSE POWER through the 1840s and 1850s; under this map's rule 5 the horse years are not drawn, which is why this feature stops in 1841 and the Chambersburg-Hagerstown line does not reappear until the 1860 rebuild. Frequency estimated, unsourced. SOURCE CONFLICT on when the horses came: pennsyrr.com puts the horse era at 1841-1860, another account has locomotives replaced by horse teams in 1844; the earlier, shorter drawn span is used here.

properties.line: Mont Alto Rail Road: Chambersburg – Mont Alto
properties.speed_source: estimated: narrow valley branch serving iron works and a picnic park; unsourced.
properties.geometry_quality: Partly approximated. 18.6 km real-traced from OpenStreetMap over the abandoned ex-PRR Waynesboro Branch ROW (Chambersburg-Fayetteville-Pond Bank), including 2.65 km of straight-line bridging where the ROW is untagged; the final 3.5 km Pond Bank-Mont Alto is a STRAIGHT LINE because OpenStreetMap carries no trace of it. Total 22.1 km / 13.8 mi.

segments.note: The Mont Alto Rail Road opened from Chambersburg east through Fayetteville and south to Mont Alto in October 1872, built to reach the Mont Alto iron works. From 1875 it also carried picnickers to Mont Alto Park, which the iron company opened on its own ground - excursion traffic that lasted until 1913. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

Chambersburg-Fayetteville-Mont Alto-Waynesboro, about 18 miles. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

properties.line: Chambersburg & Gettysburg Electric: Chambersburg – Caledonia Park
properties.speed_source: estimated: 5 ft 2.5 in gauge single-truck interurban cars on a hilly turnpike alignment; unsourced.
properties.geometry_quality: APPROXIMATED, not a traced rail alignment. Nothing of this trolley survives in OpenStreetMap, so the route is drawn along the modern highway the cars ran beside/on (US 30, the Lincoln Highway / Lincoln Way East), which is where the sources put them but is not the surveyed alignment - side-of-road private right of way would have run tens of metres off this line, and street trackage in town centres would have used a specific street pair not reconstructed here. 15.9 km / 9.9 mi drawn; no independent mileage was found to check it against.

segments.note: An electric interurban east from Chambersburg through Fayetteville to Caledonia State Park. Construction began in 1903 but disputes with the Pennsylvania Railroad over crossings held the opening to 1905; the planned extension over the mountain to Gettysburg was never built because of the grades, so despite the company name the cars never reached Gettysburg. It ran until 21 December 1926. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

properties.company: Chambersburg, Greencastle and Waynesboro Street Railway
properties.speed_source: estimated: broad-gauge interurban cars, part street running and part side-of-road; unsourced.
properties.geometry_quality: APPROXIMATED, not a traced rail alignment. Nothing of this trolley survives in OpenStreetMap, so the route is drawn along the modern highway the cars ran beside/on (US 11 (Molly Pitcher Highway) Chambersburg-Marion-Greencastle and PA 16 Greencastle-Shady Grove-Waynesboro-Rouzerville), which is where the sources put them but is not the surveyed alignment - side-of-road private right of way would have run tens of metres off this line, and street trackage in town centres would have used a specific street pair not reconstructed here. 40.0 km / 24.9 mi drawn; 85% of it follows those two routes, the remainder being connectors through town centres. No independent route mileage was found to check it against.

segments.note: The system started at Greencastle in December 1903, reached Shady Grove by 1906 and Chambersburg in 1908 - the year drawn here, because that is when Chambersburg got the cars. From Chambersburg they ran south by Marion to Greencastle, east to Shady Grove (where a Union Station met the standard-gauge Hagerstown and Frederick Railway - no interchange was possible, the two used different gauges) and on through Waynesboro to Rouzerville. Most of the system stopped on 31 July 1928. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

properties.line: Chambersburg, Greencastle & Waynesboro: Rouzerville – Pen Mar
properties.speed_source: estimated: steep, sharply curved mountain climb to the resort; unsourced.
properties.geometry_quality: APPROXIMATED, not a traced rail alignment. Nothing of this trolley survives in OpenStreetMap, so the route is drawn along the modern highway the cars ran beside/on (PA 16 east of Rouzerville), which is where the sources put them but is not the surveyed alignment - side-of-road private right of way would have run tens of metres off this line, and street trackage in town centres would have used a specific street pair not reconstructed here. 3.1 km / 2.0 mi drawn. The real trolley took its own graded alignment up the mountain, which the modern road only loosely follows.

segments.note: The climb from Rouzerville up South Mountain to Pen Mar and Blue Ridge Summit - steep grades and sharp curves - served the Pen Mar resort. It went with the rest of the system on 31 July 1928, four years before the Chambersburg-Rouzerville cars. Frequency estimated, unsourced.
